title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
claim: Holding the target problem fixed while varying only its presentation isolates extraneous load from intrinsic task difficulty, across several controlled factors.
layout: 3 panels: two top (concept, controlled comparison), five-factor mosaic below; color-coded groups
description: The figure has three parts. Panel (a), top left, shows a prompt card with a dark TARGET block that contains a small box-to-box chain. Intrinsic load is labeled on the left and points to the target. A bracket on the right labels the surrounding prompt text as extraneous load. Panel (b), top right, is a flow diagram. Low-load and high-load prompts each go through the same LLM to an Answer box. The low-load prompt has only the TARGET. The high-load prompt adds grey filler bars. A dotted line marks 'same model', and a bracket on the right says 'Compare accuracy'. Panel (c), bottom, is a mosaic of five numbered cards on tinted backgrounds. The factors are distractor quantity (K=1 to 50), distractor similarity (colorful versus uniformly red items), task interference (none, memory, counting, arithmetic), discontinuity (ordered versus shuffled numbered chains) and underspecification (explicit versus vague references). Dark navy TARGET blocks anchor the eye throughout.
caption: Isolating the effects of prompt presentation with CogLoadBench. (a) Intrinsic load comes from the task itself; extraneous load comes from how it is presented. (b) CogLoadBench keeps the target problem fixed and changes only its presentation, so comparing a model's accuracy under low and high load isolates the effect of extraneous load. (c) We vary five presentation factors, one at a time.
abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
